title: Front-loop-only treble — FLO tr
subtitle: Open, airy texture from a tall stitch in the front loop
excerpt: FLO tr inserts into the front loop only of each treble, leaving the back loop as a free ridge. At treble height the freed back loops are larger and more prominent than in FLO dc or FLO htr, creating an open, lattice-like texture used in draping shawls and open stitch panels.

glossaryTerms.definition: Treble worked into the front loop only. The back loop is freed as a prominent ridge. At treble height, the free loops are large enough to create an open, slightly lacy texture.

heroPrompt: A crochet swatch in pale blue DK yarn showing multiple rows of FLO tr, with open airy texture and visible back loop ridges, close-up.

content.text: applies the front-loop-only principle to the treble. Because the treble is a full stitch height taller than dc, the freed back loops are larger and create a noticeably open texture — closer to a lacy openwork panel than the firm rib that FLO dc produces. Used where a light, airy texture is wanted without a full lace pattern.
Work a foundation row of standard tr.
Ch 3, turn. Yarn over. Insert the hook into the front loop only of the first tr top.
Yarn over and draw up a loop (3 loops on hook). [Yarn over, draw through 2 loops] twice.
Continue FLO tr across. The back loops of the previous row stand free as open ridges.

items.symptom: Fabric is too open and unstable
items.cause: The freed back loops at treble height create a naturally open mesh
items.fix: Go down one hook size to tighten the texture, or use a heavier yarn weight. FLO tr is most stable in DK or aran — it can be too floppy in lace weight.

content.text: BLO tr puts the ridge on the right side from the same technique. For tall-stitch textured panels in crochet, front-post treble (FPTR) gives a stronger, more defined raised line than FLO tr.
